verdicts.reason: About 736,900 cochlear implants worldwide by Dec 2019 (1 million by 2022), effective for many; but this is a small share of the tens of millions with severe-to-profound loss, and adult uptake among candidates in the US is low. Measurable, well established, below mainstream.

evidence.title: Cochlear Implants (NIDCD)
evidence.shows: About 736,900 devices implanted worldwide as of Dec 2019; US about 118,100 adults and 65,000 children.

evidence.title: Quick Statistics About Hearing (NIDCD)
evidence.shows: More than 1 million implants worldwide by July 2022.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 paraplegic and some quadriplegic people routinely walk and climb stairs with computer-controlled nerve stimulation and exoskeletons.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16 mainstream: at least 20% of paraplegic people walking with such systems; 5% for partial.
verdicts.reason: Medical exoskeletons (ReWalk, first FDA approval 2014) are rehabilitation and limited personal-use devices used by a very small fraction of people with spinal cord injury; wheelchairs remain the norm.

evidence.title: Powered exoskeleton (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: ReWalk among the first FDA-approved exoskeletons for paralysed patients (2014); adoption limited by comfort, fit, control and training; no figures showing routine use.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 blindness, deafness and paraplegia are generally not noticeable and not regarded as significant disabilities.
verdicts.reason: Assistive technologies remained niche (retinal implants a few hundred users, exoskeletons rare, cochlear implants a small share of candidates); these disabilities remained significant.

evidence.title: Argus retinal prosthesis (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: The main retinal implant gave only very low-resolution vision and was discontinued in 2020.

evidence.title: Cochlear Implants (NIDCD)
evidence.shows: About 737,000 implants worldwide by 2019, a small fraction of people with severe hearing loss.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 you can do virtually anything with anyone regardless of distance, using easy, ever-present technology.
verdicts.reason: Video calling became easy and ubiquitous (Zoom grew from 10 million to more than 300 million daily meeting participants Dec 2019-Apr 2020), covering talk, work and school, but physical activities with others (the book's examples include touch) are not possible remotely. Partly true.

evidence.title: Zoom (software) (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Daily meeting participants rose from 10 million (Dec 2019) to more than 300 million (Apr 2020).

verdicts.reading: By 2019 phone calls routinely include high-resolution 3D images shown through direct-eye displays and auditory lenses.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16 mainstream: at least 20% of calls.
verdicts.reason: Calls in 2019-2024 were voice or flat 2D video on screens; direct-eye displays never became common.

evidence.title: Optical head-mounted display (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Head-mounted see-through displays had no major commercial success.

evidence.title: Zoom (software) (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Mass remote communication in 2020 ran on flat-screen video calls.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 three-dimensional holographic displays have emerged (exist as products).
verdicts.reason: Emergence claim. Glasses-free 3D light-field displays marketed as holographic existed by 2018-2021 (e.g., Google's Starline uses a 65-inch light-field display, 2021), but true diffraction holographic displays remained prototypes; MIT's 2013 forecast of mass-market holographic displays within ten years did not hold. Partly true.

evidence.title: Holographic display (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Holographic displays in prototype phase (micromagnetic piston, MIT holo-TV); 2012 car navigation display; mass market predicted within ten years of 2013.

evidence.title: Project Starline / Google Beam (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: 2021 prototype uses a 65-inch light-field display to show people in 3D.

verdicts.reading: By 2019, in 3D calls, users routinely feel as if physically near the other person.
verdicts.reason: Only research prototypes achieved this (Google Starline, shown 2021, first commercial unit 2025 at about USD 25,000); routine calls were flat video. Not true by 2024 in routine use.

evidence.title: Project Starline / Google Beam (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Announced May 2021; corporate tests from late 2022; first commercial product HP Dimension in 2025 at USD 24,999.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 the resolution of telepresence (3D call) images equals or exceeds optimal human visual acuity.
verdicts.reason: Routine video calls in 2019-2021 ran at 720p-1080p on flat screens, well below the acuity of a person in the room; acuity-level 3D telepresence did not exist outside prototypes.

evidence.title: Project Starline / Google Beam (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: The most lifelike 3D telepresence system was a 2021 prototype, commercial only in 2025.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 people can be fooled about whether another person is physically present or projected.
verdicts.reason: No telepresence system in routine use by 2024 was mistaken for physical presence; 3D booths remained prototypes or expensive enterprise products.

evidence.title: Project Starline / Google Beam (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Booth-based 3D telepresence commercial only from 2025, at about USD 25,000.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 the majority of meetings no longer require people to be physically together.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16: majority of meetings held remotely (decade rule: true by 2021).
verdicts.reason: In 2020-2021 meetings moved online at scale: Zoom rose to 300 million daily meeting participants by April 2020; in Sept 2021 45% of US full-time employees and 67% of white-collar workers worked fully or partly remotely, so most office meetings did not require proximity. True by 2021, though driven by the pandemic and not in 2019 itself.

evidence.title: Zoom (software) (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: More than 300 million daily meeting participants in April 2020, up from 10 million in Dec 2019.

evidence.title: Remote Work Persisting and Trending Permanent (Gallup)
evidence.shows: Sept 2021: 45% of US full-time employees and 67% of white-collar workers fully or partly remote.

verdicts.reading: By 2019 high-quality speech-to-speech translation for most common language pairs is routinely available in communication technology.
verdicts.mainstream_test: D16: routinely available on mainstream devices (availability, not use share).
verdicts.reason: Speech-to-speech conversation translation was routinely available on phones from 2011 (Google Translate Conversation Mode, 32 languages by 2013), in Pixel Buds (2017, 40 languages), with neural MT improving quality from 2016. Quality was uneven ('varies greatly across languages'), so 'high-quality' is the weak point.

evidence.title: Google Translate (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Conversation Mode from Jan 2011; voice translation in 32 languages by May 2013; accuracy varies greatly across languages; neural MT improved major pairs.

evidence.title: Pixel Buds (Wikipedia)
evidence.shows: Real-time translation of 40 languages via Google Assistant; reviewers found it cumbersome.
